name: Creatine Monohydrate
lead: Creatine is an organic compound that helps regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) in muscle and brain tissue. Its phosphorylated form, phosphocreatine, donates a phosphate group to ADP in a reaction catalysed by creatine kinase. The body makes it from glycine and arginine in the liver and kidneys, and about 95 percent of total body creatine sits in skeletal muscle.[1] Creatine monohydrate is the most widely sold supplemental form.

It is among the most researched sports supplements. Wikipedia reports that supplementation raises muscle phosphocreatine stores, enhances short bursts of high-intensity exercise and supports strength adaptations, with a 2018 review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition naming creatine monohydrate the most effective supplement for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and muscle mass during training.[1] A 2024 meta-analysis of resistance-training trials in adults under 50 found greater upper- and lower-body strength gains with creatine than placebo.[2]

In looksmaxxing and physique communities it is used for muscle size and fullness, and it is also the subject of recurring questions about hair loss, kidney effects and whether it counts as a steroid. Researchers have examined each of these.[3][4][5]
infobox: From glycine and arginine, with S-adenosylmethionine [1]
Dietary supplement; not a controlled substance

paras: Lifters take creatine to increase muscle mass and training performance. Wikipedia reports that it can increase maximal power and performance in repeated high-intensity work by about 5 to 15 percent.[1] On T Nation, users mention it as a staple supplement alongside protein and note that people sometimes confuse it with steroids; one poster describes hearing that it is a steroid and cheating.[6][7]
Vegetarians and vegans have lower muscle creatine levels, and Wikipedia notes that athletes on these diets may benefit from supplementation.[1]

Genetic defects in creatine synthesis or transport cause severe neurological disorders. Creatine has also been studied for cognition, depression, bone health and recovery. A 2023 meta-analysis of eight randomized trials found that creatine improved memory performance in healthy individuals, and a 2024 meta-analysis reviewed cognitive function in adults; Wikipedia says the strongest effects seem to be in stressed or cognitively impaired people and that the benefit for depressive symptoms is probably not clinically significant.[1][8][9][10]

Strength and muscle: the 2024 meta-analysis included 23 studies (mostly males) and reported mean advantages of about 4.4 kg in upper-body and 11.4 kg in lower-body strength with creatine plus resistance training compared with placebo.[2] Trials have also examined recovery from eccentric exercise-induced muscle damage, creatine nitrate with caffeine, creatine in women's health, and a two-year trial on postmenopausal bone health with exercise.[11][12][13][14] Registered studies compare monohydrate with hydrochloride in elite team-sport athletes and examine other forms.[15][16]

Hair: a 12-week randomized controlled trial published in 2025 tested the effects of creatine supplementation on androgen levels and hair follicle health in healthy people, reflecting the concern that creatine might raise dihydrotestosterone; before it, the question had no direct evidence.[17] A 2021 review of common questions about creatine addressed hair loss along with water retention, the steroid question, kidney damage, cramping and dehydration, concluding that creatine is generally well tolerated at recommended doses of 3 to 5 g per day.[3]

Kidney: a 2019 meta-analysis of six studies found creatine did not alter urea values and concluded it did not induce renal damage at the studied amounts and durations, although its pooled serum creatinine standardised difference was reported as increased; a 2025 meta-analysis of 12 studies reported a small statistically significant rise in serum creatinine.[4][5] Creatine is converted to creatinine, so creatinine can rise without kidney injury, which is the basis of discussion in these papers.

Wikipedia reports that several studies show creatine supplements decrease or at least do not increase musculoskeletal injury, cramping and dehydration.[1] The ISSN position stand and its 2021 follow-up review safety and efficacy across exercise, sport and medicine, and a 2021 review addresses use in children and adolescents.[3][18] Gastrointestinal discomfort and weight gain from water retention in muscle are commonly discussed effects, and people with kidney disease are typically advised by clinicians to consult a physician; this is a general safety fact and is not a dosing instruction.

The phosphagen system uses phosphocreatine to rapidly regenerate ATP during short, intense efforts. Supplementation can raise muscle creatine content from about 120 mmol per kg of dry muscle toward 160, and uptake is increased by insulin, IGF-1 and exercise.[1]

Absolute oral bioavailability is unknown, time to peak blood levels ranges from under an hour to about four hours depending on dose, and the elimination half-life is reported as 0.68 to 2.9 hours. Creatine is converted to creatinine and phosphocreatine and excreted by the kidneys.[1]

Michel Eugene Chevreul isolated creatine from muscle extract in 1832 and named it from the Greek word for meat. Otto Folin and Willey Glover Denis found in 1912 that ingestion could raise muscle creatine, and phosphocreatine was reported in 1927. It reached public view after the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, when The Times reported that sprinter Linford Christie had used it; EAS introduced a strength-oriented supplement called Phosphagen in 1993.[1]

lore.intro: Creatine is a near-universal baseline supplement in lifting communities, and the discussion centres on whether it is a steroid, whether it causes hair loss or kidney damage, and whether it is worth taking.[6][7]

claims.claim: Creatine is a steroid or cheating
claims.believers: Lifters report being told by outsiders that creatine is a steroid and that rapid physique change requires steroids.[7]
claims.experts: Creatine is a naturally occurring amino-acid derivative made in the body; a 2021 review specifically addresses and rejects the idea that it is an anabolic steroid.[1][3]

claims.claim: Creatine causes hair loss by raising DHT
claims.believers: The belief circulates widely in training and appearance communities and appears in common-question lists.[3]
claims.experts: A 12-week randomized trial published in 2025 tested creatine's effect on androgen levels and hair follicle health after noting no prior direct evidence.[17]

claims.believers: Posters and outsiders cite elevated creatinine on blood tests as proof of harm.[3]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report no renal damage at studied doses and durations, with a small rise in serum creatinine reported in the 2025 analysis.[4][5]

claims.believers: Lifters treat it as a basic supplement for performance and size.[6]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis found larger strength gains with creatine plus resistance training than placebo.[2]

claims.believers: A T Nation psychology thread discusses a newsletter item on creatine as a possible treatment for depression.[19]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report improved memory in healthy people, and a 2023 randomized trial examined cognitive performance; reviewers describe results across domains as conflicting.[1][8][20]
